items.note: Story 1: Association organized 1889 at Larrow Green, creamery built 1891; Gideon Vose named (Story 4, 'son of Gideon Vose who had organized the Association').
Gives 'paid according to butter-fat test, not milk weight' but never states the second required half: the test of the station where he delivers governs.
Only 'a decision that became the hinge of all that followed'; never states that payment by test is what made a wrong test cost money.
Only Hobart Sill (as 'a buttermaker') appears; no Effie Loomis, no Wilbur Teague. Core officer fact absent.
Story 4: 'Selby Vose, the manager—son of Gideon Vose'. Start year absent in A (and given wrongly as 1911 in B/D, deducted separately).
The station-gain ledger line appears nowhere in Section A (only in B3/C3/D2); credit does not travel into A.
Ostrey Hollow station, seven miles up the valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glass borrowed from Larrow Green — all in Story 1.
Weighed in, sampled, tested, cream to Larrow Green, skim returned; 17.6 c.c. charge into a bottle whose neck is ruled for that volume.
Ammon & Sons of Tarnet, invoice 14 April 1897, in use May 1897.
6 dozen pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., 12 dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93 — exact.
Story 2: 'constant at nineteen hundredths of a point in every month, wet February and dry June alike'.
Never states that a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, of which there was none in the county.
Keddie tester from 1896, 'twenty-nine seasons', dismissed 30 April 1925; died 1934.
The station test book in Keddie's hand is named (Stories 3 and 6); bold gates on the test book, the column list is context.
No summary leaf; 3.61 given but the 1896 figure of 3.80 never appears in Section A. Both figures required.
Pipette broke 8 May 1911, borrowed measure nine weeks to 10 July, tests higher then fell back, question mark set. (3.80 value missing but scored at D1.3.)
Story 4: 'Emmet was Orra's brother ... the largest patron ... the one who lost the most by the low tests'; Orra is Keddie's wife.
1919 circular over the manager's signature present, but Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement ('tested as I was taught, cannot say why') is absent from Section A. Both halves required.
Died 13 February 1934, cleared only in 1958 — still under the imputation.
Own aspect (six farms with rights on Hessel Bottom) never given; Brant-as-largest already scored at A3.5 and cannot be scored twice.
Brant's weigh book named only as an exhibit; no 1 January 1897 start, no statement that the two scales agreed. The double-weighing is misattributed to Keddie.

1902 complaints present, but the run conflates the two gaps: it prints Larrow Green 3.78 against 3.61 and calls the deficiency nineteen hundredths, and Story 3 says the figures ran 'nineteen hundredths below everywhere else'. The key charges this loss.
1908 committee mentioned, but Nyle Grigg is unnamed and the Jan-Mar 1908 sampling window is absent. (Finding correctly hedged, so no corruption deduction.)
Brant's 1910 year absent from Section A; C2 explicitly says the figure cannot be found and estimates 140,000 lb.
Nothing on the weigh book passing to Roy Brant in 1929 or being lent to Ivy in 1958.
Alder Corners, Redlow Ridge, Vessey County and Jerome Cudd appear nowhere in Section A.
No four patrons hauling to Alder Corners in the summer flush from 1915.
No statement of the test's independence; the cheese factory is mentioned only in D2/F, which cannot credit Section A.
No sixteen overlapping seasons, no 0.19 differential at Alder Corners in Section A.
The 'same milk in two buildings' argument is made only in Sections D and F.
Rosalie Cudd is named only in D2/F, not in Section A; her copying of sixteen seasons for Ivy is never mentioned.
Strawn named and his disinterest stated, but the Ordell circuit 1907-1936 is absent (and 1908 is asserted elsewhere).
Lactometer run for added water and none ever found at Ostrey Hollow (Stories 4 and 6). Wrong start year deducted separately.
12 June 1923, pipettes run against a calibrated burette, whole lot condemned.
'He wrote down ... that the glass had been condemned. He drew no inference as to the years behind it.'
Order of 28 June and reply of 2 July are right, but the 1924 average is given as 3.85. A wrong 1924 average loses the item (key: r08's 3.90 loses it).
Crate carried to the loft over the intake room in 1923; notebooks with the state dairy office. (1947 college library missing, but that is not a stated both-required pair.)
'By January 1925 ... the Ostrey Hollow patrons ... filed a formal petition' — the date carries the item.
Board under Alonzo Frick, three sittings, two of them in the station's weigh room. (Session dates appear in Section E.)
Three explanations argued — watering (Vose), theft by the operator, bog hay — and the finding found nothing, 'without admission' of any cause.
Exactly the four books, including Strawn's 1923 notebook.
Dismissed 30 April 1925 without a finding; award of 4 May 1925, $3,800, 'without admission', charged to the station account.
No one-fifth-of-$19,000 statement and no identity with the station-gain account; the run gives $19,600 and never links the award to the gain line.
Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, Duncan's daughter, graduate student in dairy husbandry at Farland; Leland Vaught named in Story 8.
Only Strawn's notebooks are named as retrieved; no assembly of records that had never been in the same room.
February 1958 and the loft are right, but 'Eleven of the original pipettes were still intact' — nine is required and gates the item.
9 March 1958 and the burette are right, but the mean is given as 16.27 c.c., short 1.33 / 7.6 percent, instead of 16.72 / 0.88 / 0.95.
Says only 'always the same proportion, nineteen hundredths'; no 95-percent-of-true reading, no 3.61-where-3.80-stood, no 0.19 = 5 percent of 3.80.
All four required elements fail: no 25 full years 1898-1922, no 76,000 lb, $19,600 not $19,000, and no ledger identity.
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, states the cause and clears him; 'twenty-four years too late' after his death.
Granddaughter.
Derivation through Duncan given, with Duncan's own family record and the editor's correction.
Second cousins with the full derivation through Emmet/Orra and Roy/Duncan.
Abstention item A08: the full-vs-half sibling question of Emmet and Orra is never raised, so the required declared inability is absent. No assertion either, so no gullibility deduction.
Selby was Gideon's son, not nephew.
Significance missed: no link to Article VII making the station's test decide pay (only 'architect of its bylaws'), and no Vose-Jerseys-lost-most alternative.

Abstention item A01 asserted: 'Duncan's explicit, documented denial ... outweighs Cleve's unsubstantiated hearsay' and 'the most reliable conclusion is that no proven relationship existed' — a verdict sentence resolving it by weighing narrators, exactly what the key forbids ('a family member's denial is not a record').
States what is established: Duncan's flat denial, Cleve's second-hand talk, and no documentary support anywhere.
Gives 7.6 percent short / 92.4 percent of mark from the planted 16.27; the answer is 0.95 and 5 percent.
3.80 true average, short 0.19 — both figures match, though derived backwards from an assumed 0.19 and inconsistent with its own 7.6 percent.
80,000 lb (from a miscomputed 1,440,000), and then declines between 67,000 and 80,000. Key answer 76,000 lb.
$19,600 and 19.4 percent — the NT-8 diagnostic exactly. Key answer $19,000 and one fifth.
Says the 1910 delivery is not in the sources and estimates 140,000 lb → 5,054 lb. Key answer 6,840 lb from 200,000 lb at 3.42.
266 lb from the estimate. Key answer 360 lb.
Misreads the station gain as shrinkage in transit and gets 1,364,400 lb received. Key answer 1,520,000 lb actually delivered.
75,600 lb / 5.25 percent of the credited amount. Key answer 76,000 lb, 5.00 percent of fat delivered or 5.26 percent of fat credited.
Itemized to $77.93, and correctly notes the $77.39 carriers fail against the sum.
72 pipettes right, but the shortfall per pipette is given as 1.33 c.c.; 0.88 c.c. required and both elements gate.

26 years and ~41 days is close on the span, but the full delivery years are given as '1897-1923 = 26 complete years'. Key requires 25 full years 1898-1922 alongside 26 years 6 weeks; one number for both = 0.
Abstention item A02 asserted: 'First season milk (1896-1897): approximately 1,100,000 pounds' from Kyle's memory.
Variable named as the measuring glass / pipette; 'Only the glass had changed'.
Herds, pasture, tester, season, machinery, procedure held constant — well over three.
Result given only as 'markedly higher' and 'fell back to their former level'; the required 3.80 through the interval and 3.61 on 10 July are absent.
States the cause lies in the glass and not the milk, herds, pasture or tester's honesty, and states limits (magnitude of the error, why the glass was short, how long it had been defective).
Three distinct valid reasons — the 1911 interval (Falke), the ledger showing no deficit (Kyle), the same herds testing high at the cheese factory (Cudd) — three different narrators.
States reason 1 is independent of any later measurement of the glass and reason 3 would hold if 1911 had never occurred; each rests on a different source.

Abstention item A09 asserted: 'Kyle did not voice doubt about the ledger entries at the time', 'named, explained as routine loss, and therefore unquestioned'. No declared inability, and the counter-narrator is never mentioned.
Answers the literal question yes — he knew the station's tests ran low — citing the 1902-onward complaints and the 1919 circular.

Three of the five established items: the signed annual ledger sheets carrying the station-gain line, the 1919 water circular, and (in F2) his advancing the watering explanation. The 1913 start is given wrongly as 1911.

Abstention item A03: says only that whether he understood the cause 'is less certain' — a hedge, not a declared inability, and none of the two required supporting observations are given at the question. No -2, since its verdict sentences stay on item-1 ground ('tests ran low', 'the fact of the shortfall').

Capped at 3, earned by: the 1897 vs 1898 installation date resolved to 1 May 1897 on the invoice and the diary; $3,500 vs $3,800 resolved to $3,800 on the record against a second-hand memory; first-cousins-once-removed vs second cousins resolved by derivation. (Great-niece is scored at E-b instead, never both.)

Capped at 3: great-niece carried by both R19 and R22 with R22's own correction as breaker; Bulletin 214's 'two tenths' carried by both Grigg (R15) and Kepp (R16), broken by the bulletin itself; $77.39 noted as carried by more than one source and broken by summing the itemized transcription.
None of A04, A06, A10 is stated as unsettleable with what the sources do establish. A04 is left as loose speculation about the mold, A06 never asks whose measure was borrowed, A10 is untouched.
The one attempt (Cleve Oram) is explicitly withdrawn: 'This is not a direct logical contradiction within Cleve's account.' No narrator is identified refuting itself on the page.
Names the 1897 pipettes and the onset/cessation, but the size is wrong throughout — 16.27 c.c., 7.6 percent — and 0.19 is never derived as 5 percent of 3.80.
Names the watering explanation (Selby Vose, 1919) and defeats it with Strawn's lactometer on every visit and the same milk testing 3.78-3.82 at the cheese factory.
Names the theft explanation and defeats it with the 1911 interval under the same operator and the absence of any ledger deficit.
Names the bog-hay explanation (1908 committee, Dr. Kepp) and defeats it with Bulletin 214's five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer against a flat 0.19, plus the ridge comparison.
Abstention item A07 asserted: the answer opens 'No.' — a headline verdict. The key requires a declared inability whatever way the evidence leans.
Abstention item A05 asserted: 'Ansel Keddie suspected the glass beginning in summer 1911 ... carried the private suspicion to his death', resting on the son's uncorroborated recollection.
161 words against a 150-word cap.
Names at most one record series (the 1958 measurement); no minute book, invoice, test book, weigh book, cheese-factory book, notebooks, arbitration minutes or ledgers.
Decoys are correctly held at arm's length, but the headline number is wrong and self-contradictory: 'delivering only 95% of their marked capacity—causing all tests to read 7.6% low'.
Four of six arc elements covering both ends: one part in twenty (95 percent of marked capacity), 1897, 1923 with no inference drawn, 1958. Loses the 76,000 lb / $19,000 element and both names.

deductions.reason: Asserts the pipettes' mean delivery as 16.27 c.c. (F033, NT-1) throughout Section A, C1 and F1
Asserts the loss as $19,600 (F081) in Story 8 and C1(d)
Asserts eleven surviving pipettes (F089, NT-16) in Story 7
Asserts the 1919 circular was carried to eleven families (F058) in Story 4 and D3
Asserts Selby Vose became manager in 1911 (catalogued planted error) in B3 and D3
Asserts Strawn's lactometer visits ran 'from 1908 forward', i.e. the 1908 circuit start (catalogued planted error), in Story 6 and F2
Asserts the 1924 station average as 3.85 (catalogued planted error) in Story 5
Gullibility: abstention item A01 (Vose-Keddie kinship) resolved by weighing narrators
Gullibility: abstention item A02 (1896 first-season intake) asserted as ~1,100,000 lb
Gullibility: abstention item A05 (what the tester believed) asserted — he suspected the glass from 1911
Gullibility: abstention item A07 (did the 1925 board examine the glassware) answered 'No.'
Gullibility: abstention item A09 (whether the bookkeeper ever questioned the entries) asserted — he never voiced doubt
